newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-Deutsche upbeat despite MGAM charge.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Deutsche upbeat despite MGAM charge.

text.p: Germany's Deutsche Bank AG on Wednesday revealed it had to pay more than a billion marks ($593.5 million) to sort out the 1996 mismanagement scandal at its London investment funds unit MGAM, but said it was optimistic for the year ahead.
Conceding that it needed to do more to prove itself a global player in investment banking, the German giant nonetheless downplayed the MGAM saga as a one-off.
"For 1997 we are confident overall," chief executive Hilmar Kopper told a news conference, as he gave his last major address to reporters before his retirement in May.
"We are confident that the strategic decisions and structural changes in the group, which entail considerable preliminary costs, will have an even stronger positive impact in 1997," Kopper added.
Deutsche reported a 37 percent rise in operating profit for 1996 to 5.8 billion marks. Its net income advanced 4.6 percent to 2.2 billion, depressed by a surge in tax costs.
Kopper said 1996 was a good year overall, although interest income was pressured by continued low interest rates, and a "highly successful year" for asset management.

But the bank was still forced to set aside between 1.1 and 1.2 billion marks to cover damages related to Morgan Grenfell Asset Management, pushing its extraordinary expenses item up to 1.49 billion marks from 377 million marks. The expenses were offset by profits from investments of roughly the same amount.
"We don't know yet exactly (what the costs will be), the calculations are still continuing," Kopper said.

The charge stems from the three-day suspension of three mutual funds in September due to irregularities centring on unquoted securities. Peter Young, the portfolio manager responsible for two of the funds, was dismissed and four other managers left the company over the affair.
Deutsche previously estimated that compensating investors would cost about 200 million pounds ($323.5 million) on top of a net injection into the funds of 180 million pounds.
But Kopper said his optimism for 1997 was based on strong operating income and trading earnings for the first two months. Low interest rates would likely keep lending demand buoyant.
Own-account trading profit jumped 58.5 percent to 3.2 billion marks in 1996 and has tripled in the last three years to now account for 15 percent of regular income.
But at the same time, Kopper predicted rising competition, continued pressure on margins, high costs "and hardly any reduction in the need for risk provisioning."
The bank's net risk provisions for 1996 fell to 800 million marks from 1.4 billion marks the previous year.
The bank also needed to develop its investment bank Deutsche Morgan Grenfell, particularly in Europe and Asia.
"Deutsche Morgan Grenfell has not yet reached the end of its build-up phase, but future expansion will continue to be monitored and focused," Deutsche said.

But Kopper as usual brushed aside renewed calls for Deutsche to cut down its massive network of industrial holdings, which unions and many politicians see as symptomatic of German banks' unhealthy dominance of industry.
"As long as the tax situation remains unchanged, we won't sell. If the situation changes, we will have to rethink," Kopper said, referring to tax charges on equity sales.

He said Deutsche's purchase of a 5.21 percent stake in Bayerische Vereinsbank AG last year, a move which unleashed merger speculation mania in Germany, was "one of the better investments" of 1996 in terms of its share performance.
"We wanted to throw our hat into the ring and said 'We will look at Vereinsbank,'" Kopper added, refusing to be drawn about the future shape of the German banking industry.

Deutsche's shares outperformed on Wednesday, rising 2.4 marks to 93.67 marks while the blue chip DAX index advanced two percent. The German banking sector has come back into vogue in recent days on the back of persistent merger talk.
Hilmar Kopper took over as chief executive of Deutsche Bank in 1989 after his predecessor Alfred Herrhausen was killed in an attack by left-wing terrorists.

He will be succeeded at the bank's helm in May by Rolf Breuer, a prominent figure in Frankfurt financial circles and now a board member at the bank. ($ = 1.685 German Marks) ($ = 0.618 British Pounds)
